items.title: Don’t say it’s green! How green framing can depress support for renewable energy
items.summary_raw: Abstract The green transition implies a shift towards renewable energies. However, their deployment has faced some backlash. This article assesses whether (a) the type of renewables and (b) framing can affect support for deployment. Through a survey experiment, three types of renewables (hydropower, onshore wind, offshore wind) and three types of frames (energy sovereignty, economic competitiveness, green transition) are evaluated, in general and for two typically skeptical groups (the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites). Using the case of Norway, we find strong effects for the type of renewables but little evidence for general framing effects. There are two exceptions: green framing has a negative effect on support for renewables where citizens have more fluid preferences (offshore wind) and depresses support among the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites. For these citizens, remaining silent about the climate benefits of renewable energy will actually boost support for its deployment.

items.title: Indicator-based diagnosis of carbon metabolism in production–living–ecological spaces: Land-use transitions, ecological network relationships, and terrain-constrained carbon flows in the Nanling Mountains, China
items.summary_raw: Land-use changes among production–living–ecological (PLE) spaces are critical drivers of regional carbon metabolism. Although these changes have been extensively examined in urban agglomerations and plains, their carbon metabolic mechanisms in mountainous areas remain inadequately explored. In this study, ecological network analysis (ENA) was used to identify ecological interactions among PLE spatial categories and evaluate the utility of the carbon metabolism network. In addition, the topographic constraints on major negative carbon flow pathways were examined. The results reveal the following. (1) Ecological spaces continuously dominated the Nanling Mountains during the full study period. From 2000 to 2020, total carbon emissions increased from 14.46 million t C to 25.18 million t C, whereas total carbon sinks remained relatively stable. (2) The carbon metabolism network was dominated by competitive and control/exploitation relationships. The overall utility values for 2000–2010 and 2010–2020 were 0.690 and 0.815, respectively, both below 1.0. In the latter period, competitive relationships decreased, whereas mutualistic relationships increased; this indicates a slight improvement in network relationships, although negative network effects still predominated. (3) The conversion of forest ecological spaces and agricultural production spaces into manufacturing production spaces, particularly F → M and C → M transitions, was the main driver of negative carbon flows. These…

items.title: Pakistan–US Strategic Relations: The Role of Regional Security and Institutional Alliances (NATO & SCO)
items.summary_raw: This study examines the bilateral relationship between Pakistan and the United States with a focus on military cooperation and regional security, analyzed within the broader frameworks of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and NATO. Employing a mixed-method research design, the study integrates qualitative insights and quantitative analysis using SPSS. Data were collected from 125 respondents across multiple academic institutions in Pakistan, selected through stratified random sampling to ensure diverse representation. Qualitative interview data were collected from 25 respondents, while quantitative data were obtained from 100 respondents and analyzed using regression analysis. The findings reveal that regional security is the most significant determinant of Pakistan–US relations (β = 0.452, p = 0.034), highlighting the centrality of security cooperation in shaping bilateral engagement. Gender and familiarity with the subject also show positive influences, whereas military cooperation, NATO, and SCO variables are statistically insignificant. Respondents emphasize that Pakistan–US relations are historically anchored in military cooperation, with perceived benefits for counterterrorism and regional stabilization, particularly in Afghanistan. However, concerns persist regarding fluctuating trust, geopolitical tensions, and shifting regional power dynamics involving China and India. The study concludes that Pakistan–US relations are characterized by both cooperation and…

items.title: Does concern for climate change impact the use of vapes or electronic cigarettes?
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Limited direct evidence suggests that climate change concern may impact e-cigarette use, particularly in populations affected by climate-related events, though broader environmental awareness also influences public attitudes towards vaping products.

items.title: Why energy poverty persists: Multidimensional evidence from contrasting energy transitions in Tanzania and Vietnam
items.summary_raw: Expanding access to modern energy does not necessarily eliminate energy poverty. Even as incomes rise and energy access improves for many households, others may continue to experience deprivation across essential energy services. Yet relatively little is known about the forms this persistence takes and how they differ across energy-transition contexts. Using nationally representative household data from Tanzania and Vietnam from 2008 to 2020, we examine these patterns through a multidimensional energy poverty index. We assess changes in the incidence, intensity, dimensions, and distribution of energy poverty, estimate household-level correlates using Tobit and Logit models, and apply an Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to the cross-country energy-deprivation gap. Energy poverty declined substantially in both countries, but persistence differed markedly. Tanzania exhibited broad persistence, with deprivation remaining widespread and severe despite major gains in electricity access, while Vietnam exhibited more residual and concentrated persistence following a rapid decline in aggregate energy poverty. Unclean cooking fuels remained the most persistent deprivation in both countries. Income, education, urban residence, and non-farm employment were associated with lower energy deprivation, while farming was associated with greater deprivation. Observable household characteristics accounted for 27.4% of the cross-country gap, indicating that differences in socioeconomic endowments…

items.title: Structural improvements to address energy poverty had most substantial thermal comfort and health effects
items.summary_raw: Abstract Interventions for energy poverty have increased in the wake of the energy crisis, with many nations attempting to ease experiences for their citizens. We use data collected as part of [redacted] which explored the impact of interventions for energy poverty and improving health in 6 European Cities. By categorising interventions into structural, small measures, advice and financial support, we can differentiate between the energy poverty and health impacts of each category. We find through our longitudinal analysis there is little, if any, effect from small home improvements and energy advice, but that structural interventions for energy poverty have some positive thermal comfort and health effects. Further, direct financial support has clear positive effects on health and energy saving practices, and when financial support fluctuates, so do participants’ living conditions. Governments should invest in a range of measures, with a recognition that structural measures and consistent financial support are most effective.

items.title: Fair Business Models for Climate‐Smart Agriculture: A Design Science Research Approach
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Organisations in agri‐food value chains face urgent demands to address climate change, environmental degradation and social inequities through climate‐smart agriculture (CSA). However, sustained CSA implementation remains constrained by business models (BMs) that fail to offer fair solutions to stakeholders. Existing business model innovation (BMI) literature lacks conceptualisation of fair BMs and methodology for operationalising fairness in BMs, leading to the research question: How can fair BMs for CSA be defined, designed and developed? Using design science research across five European case studies, the study defines a fair BM as a BM in which the design of the value proposition, creation, delivery and capture enables equitable value distribution, inclusive processes, transparency of information and respectful relationships among stakeholders. The study operationalises fairness across the BMI process with stakeholder engagement and change management, deriving eight design requirements and thirteen stakeholder‐validated prototypes. The study advances BMI literature by offering prescriptive knowledge for operationalising fairness in agri‐food BMI.

items.title: Adaptation of EU policy during geopolitical change: the impact on forest use, bioenergy, and climate security in the Baltic region
items.summary_raw: Abstract Background Forests in the Baltic Sea region store carbon, harbour biodiversity, sustain rural livelihoods and supply wood for materials and heating. Since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, sanctions on Russian and Belarusian wood and energy have disrupted these supply chains. This raises concern that the pursuit of energy security may increase pressure on forests, weaken carbon sinks and shift environmental impacts abroad. EU Member States set out how they will meet the 2030 energy and climate targets in National Energy and Climate Plans (NECPs), updated in 2024. This is the first study to examine these updates for Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Sweden through the lenses of climate security and “nexus thinking”, an approach that treats energy, land, ecosystems and society as interconnected. It combines content analysis of the five plans with 22 interviews with regional stakeholders. Results All five countries are turning to domestic bioenergy to replace Russian fuels, mainly forest residues and low-grade wood for district heating and combined heat and power. The Baltic states link forests mainly to energy sovereignty, grid integration with continental Europe and rural jobs. Sweden and Finland embed them in longer-term strategies for the bioeconomy, carbon sinks, hydrogen and carbon capture. Most plans favor using high-quality timber for products and residues for energy. Yet the plans only partly reflect the new situation: many adjustments happen in…

items.title: Impact of Layperson and Scientific Messaging on Sustainable Beef From Seaweed‐Fed Cattle
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT A discrete choice experiment was conducted to elicit consumer preferences for a sustainable beef product from cattle fed a seaweed‐supplemented diet. Additionally, two types of information treatments were tested to determine the more effective method of conveying environmental information. Findings indicate that consumers tend to discount such novel beef. However, while both information treatments significantly increased willingness to pay, the layperson's language proved significantly more effective and independent of consumers' educational background. These results imply that straightforward communication can enhance consumer acceptance of innovative, sustainable products. Policymakers and the beef industry should prioritize the use of plain language to promote environmentally friendly meat products.

items.title: Withholding One's Political Views: When, Why, and On What?
items.summary_raw: Abstract Scholarly interest in the unwillingness of people to express their political views has ballooned of late, across the world. Still, many details of when, why, and on what people self-censor remain unknown. In this largely exploratory analysis, using 2025 survey data from the United States, I pursue four objectives. First, I document the extremely high levels of self-censorship in the contemporary United States. Then I analyze the varied contexts in which people withhold their views, followed by an analysis of why they say they are reluctant to express themselves. In the most important part of my article, I examine the issues on which people are most likely to withhold their views. Distinguishing between expressed public opinion and true public opinion, I then show that on many issues self-censorship results in no ideological bias in expressed views, but on some issues—the Israeli war with Hamas, as the best example—considerable bias exists (true opinion differs from expressed opinion). I conclude with concerns about the deleterious effects of self-censorship on political discussions and deliberations in America.

items.title: Whither the climate movement (and what comes next)?
items.summary_raw: Abstract Perspectives do not contain abstracts, excerpt from the perspective: In this perspective, I provide evidence about how the climate movement has redirected its efforts given the current “nonreceptive political and social environment” to maintain some level of continuity [7]. After presenting data about how the climate movement has shifted its focus, I consider what it will take to reinvigorate the movement so it can help motivated the changes we need to address the climate crisis. Since the US is the top historical contributor to climate change and has been home to a vibrant climate movement, I present data collected from activists in the US to provide empirical context

items.title: Logic and Path of Enterprise Digitalization Empowering Low-Carbon Transition Under the Background of "Carbon Peaking and Carbon Neutrality"
items.source_name: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
items.summary_raw: Against the backdrop of intensifying global warming, achieving carbon peaking and carbon neutrality has become a common goal of economic transformation for all countries worldwide. Starting from the dual-carbon context, this paper analyzes the internal logic, practical dilemmas and optimization paths of digital technologies empowering enterprises' low-carbon transition. Digital technologies empower enterprises' low-carbon transition by integrating low-carbon information resources, innovating low-carbon technologies and optimizing industrial structure. However, there remain problems such as insufficient two-way adaptability between digitalization and low-carbon technologies, shortage of "digital-low-carbon" interdisciplinary talents, and absence of special guarantees for collaborative transformation. Multi-dimensional empowerment for enterprises' low-carbon transition can be realized by strengthening technological R&D and innovation, improving the level of technology integration and application, building a diversified talent training system, and improving the multi-dimensional support system for the integrated development of digitalization and low-carbon development in enterprises.

items.title: The impact of updating World Meteorological Organization baselines on Australian climate change messaging
items.source_name: Journal of Southern Hemisphere Earth System Science
items.summary_raw: Baselines matter in our perception of which is the climate ‘normal’ and what benchmark we use to track climate changes. Use of recent baselines grounds expectations about historical and future climates in recent lived experience, but differences between even similar recent periods shape our perceptions and interpretations of climate information. Here, we examine various examples of the effect of changing standard World Meteorological Organisation baselines (1961–90 and 1991–2020), as well as the pre-industrial baseline of 1850–1900, in the context of climate change messaging in Australia. We find the choice of baseline notably affects the messaging, with different connotations in two different contexts. The first context is where there are ongoing and attributable trends, such as in temperature, sea level and some localised precipitation changes. Here, the baseline grounds our perception of ‘normal’ to a particular point in an ongoing trend, and this normal is increasingly different from current lived experience. Also, in this context, reported ranges of change are smaller for more recent baselines. The second context is where there are weak climate change trends, and differences between baselines are primarily due to climate variability, such as most regional precipitation changes. Here, the baseline also grounds the perception of the climate ‘normal’, not as a particular point on an ongoing trend but rather in a particular state of climate variability. Here, a challenge…

items.title: A Thematic Synthesis of Social-Emotional Learning, Learning Climate, and Student Achievement in Elementary Education
items.source_name: Journal of General Education and Humanities
items.summary_raw: Social and emotional learning (SEL) is increasingly recognized as an important component of elementary education, supporting students’ social-emotional development, engagement, well-being, and academic learning. However, the relationships among teacher social-emotional competence, learning climate, implementation quality, and student outcomes remain insufficiently integrated, particularly in the Indonesian context. This study aims to synthesize literature on these relationships and examine their implications for SEL implementation in Indonesian elementary schools. A narrative literature review was conducted using an existing source corpus supplemented by relevant peer-reviewed literature. The synthesis examined major themes concerning teacher competence, classroom practices, learning climate, student outcomes, implementation conditions, and contextual adaptation. The findings suggest that teacher competence is associated with the quality of SEL enactment, while a supportive learning climate provides a context for student participation and social-emotional learning. Implementation quality and cultural context also shape how SEL is adapted and sustained. These relationships should not be interpreted as a universally established causal pathway. The review highlights the need for context-responsive teacher development, school-level support, and rigorous evaluation of SEL practices. Future empirical research in Indonesian elementary schools should investigate these relationships…

items.title: Whispers of Change: Positive Climate Communication Through ASMR and Its Potential for Climate Engagement
items.summary_raw: In recent years, interest has grown in using positive climate communication, broadly understood as climate messages designed to evoke constructive emotional, cognitive, and relational responses, such as hope, efficacy, and nature connectedness, rather than fear or anxiety, to foster climate engagement. While most research has focused on traditional journalism, Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) videos, featuring whispered content and natural soundscapes, may offer a novel sensory-affective format to complement such messages and foster reflective engagement with climate change. This study first explored participants’ reflections through an open-ended thought-listing, showing that ASMR videos can elicit appreciation of nature and personal responsibility for climate action. A 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment (N = 159) then tested whether whispered narration and nature sounds influence contentment, momentary well-being, and behavioral intentions. Quantitative analyses revealed no significant effects. However, qualitative thought-listing data suggest that ASMR may present an innovative sensory-affective format that can foster emotional engagement and reflective consideration of climate action, pointing to new directions for positive climate communication.

items.title: ‘I Love Science,’ but ‘Climate Science Completely Misses the Mark’: Understanding Criticism of Climate Science Institutions Among Those Using a Scientific Repertoire
items.summary_raw: This study aims to advance our understanding of criticism of scientific institutions by those who are scientifically oriented. To this end, we focus on a strategic case: criticism of climate science among people who use a scientific repertoire. An abductive analysis of 20 in-depth interviews highlights the existence of a ‘science confidence gap’, that is, self-ascribed affinity with modern scientific methods and principles, but distrust of climate science institutions. Our investigation illustrates how respondents equate a good scientific attitude with an individualist epistemology. Engaging in a form of boundary work, they argue that climate science institutions stifle such an individualist epistemology. More specifically, respondents identify five mechanisms that inhibit the scientific rigour of climate science: (1) ‘consensus-thinking’; (2) institutional path-dependency; (3) political agenda-setting; (4) the negativity bias inherent in the scientific endeavour; and (5) the ‘unscientificness’ of climate models. This study demonstrates empirically what a scientific critique of scientific institutions entails and how it can be understood. Our findings may inspire future research on criticism of scientific institutions in other fields.

items.title: Bibliometric Analysis of Climate Change and Agritourism Sustainability in Rural Destinations
items.summary_raw: Rural agritourism is increasingly studied in the context of climate change and sustainability. However, less attention has been paid to how it might assist local communities under pressure from climate. The research literature spans a range of topics related to tourism, agricultural adaptation, rural development and sustainability. This study examines the research structure to show how the field has developed and what topics still need more attention. Data covered publications from 1987 to 2025 and were collected on 25 December 2025. The search retrieved 216 documents from Scopus and 183 from Web of Science. After removing duplicates and one retracted document, a total of 281 documents were obtained. The study used performance analysis together with three mapping techniques. These included author co-citation, keyword co-occurrence and strategic thematic mapping. A total of 226 documents were published after 2017. They represented 80.4% of the dataset. Rural tourism and climate change became the main themes. The co-citation results identified four intellectual foundations. Tourism development and agricultural adaptation formed two foundations, whereas institutional support and climate-tourism sustainability shaped the remaining two. The keyword network highlighted farm vulnerability and tourism sustainability. Management and destination adaptation were also prominent. Basic themes offer a general framework of the field, and rural tourism and climate change are the core…

items.title: Geopolitical forces and strategic decision-making in multinational firms: a scorecard and heatmap comparative analysis
items.source_name: Technological and Economic Development of Economy
items.summary_raw: In an increasingly interconnected world, the knowledge economy-encompassing technology, education and research-faces complex challenges posed by the evolving geopolitical dynamics. This paper examines how multinational companies strategically respond to these shifts. Through a compre­hensive analysis of regulatory changes, political instability, trade policies and decarbonization concerns, this paper highlights the composite nature of geopolitical risks and their influence on corporate strate­gy. Methodologically, the research employs a scorecard and a heatmap to provide a systematic, organ­ization‑level framework for comparing firms’ strategic responses. The scorecard evaluates regulatory compliance, supply chain resilience, risk management, strategic partnerships, innovation and carbon reduction targets across Apple, SAP and Tesla, with scores ranging from 2.00 to 4.00. Apple achieves the highest overall score (3.33/4), followed by Tesla (3.00/4) and SAP (2.83/4), indicating differences in inno­vation, policy alignment and supply chain resilience. The heatmap compares TotalEnergies, Danfoss and General Electric across eight decarbonization indicators, showing Danfoss as the sustainability leader. General Electric exhibits strong renewable‑energy capabilities, but remains constrained by legacy infra­structure. By applying this comparative framework, the study identifies improvement areas and offers strategic recommendations to help multinational companies strengthen…

items.title: Do “warm glow” feelings affect climate mitigation behaviors? A field experiment on consumer electric energy choices
items.summary_raw: Abstract Addressing the climate crisis is going to require behavioral change in many aspects of daily life. A growing literature suggests the promise of “warm glow” messaging that features the pleasure and satisfaction one experiences from acting sustainably. Yet previous research has relied almost exclusively on self‐reported behavioral intentions, leaving open whether such appeals meaningfully affect real‐world, costly choices. We partnered with a local organization to conduct a field experiment on energy choices in Hanover, New Hampshire. Using a randomized roll‐out design in early 2025, we systematically varied the timing of postcard mailers that contain a warm glow message encouraging customers to increase the renewable content of their energy option. Analyses of administrative data on consumer energy choices reveal that warm glow messages delivered in a field setting have a null effect on adoption of higher‐renewable power choices, with a small number of customers changing to the greener but more costly option. Our study provides novel behavioral evidence on the real‐world impact of intrinsic motivation appeals in the climate domain.

items.title: Municipalities as learning ecosystems: Integrating local climate action into climate change education in Ankara, Türkiye
items.summary_raw: Climate change education is commonly organized through schools, yet many of the infrastructures, decisions, and public encounters through which residents learn about climate change are governed locally. Municipalities may therefore function not only as service providers but also as learning ecosystems. This study examines how local climate action can be translated into climate change education through a document-based case study of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM), Türkiye. Eleven publicly available municipal and intergovernmental documents and webpages published between 2022 and 2026 were analysed using qualitative document analysis and abductive thematic coding. The analysis combined climate change education principles, learning-city scholarship and urban climate governance research. Five mutually reinforcing dimensions were identified: policy-to-pedagogy translation, place-based practice, partnership brokerage, participation and agency, and evidence and feedback. Ankara demonstrates substantial assets across these dimensions, including formal climate plans, municipal lifelong-learning spaces, teacher education partnerships, youth and children’s participation structures, and operational sites that can serve as living laboratories. However, these assets remain only partly connected: educational objectives are not consistently embedded in climate plans, participation mechanisms are not systematically linked to implementation cycles, and evaluation largely records…

items.title: Okamurův noční manévr. Schmarcz: ČT je jen záminka, Babiš chce konflikt v ulicích
items.summary_raw: Páteční noční operace ve Sněmovně nebyla podle komentátora Martina Schmarcze jen pokusem prosadit kontroverzní novelu zákona o České televizi a Českém rozhlasu. Vládní koalice v čele s Andrejem Babišem a Tomiem Okamurou se podle něj rozhodla záměrně vyvolat politický střet, aby překryla vlastní problémy a mobilizovala své voliče. „Tohle je válka,“ říká Schmarcz v nové České jízdě a vysvětluje, proč považuje postup vlády za nebezpečný precedens, co mohou změnit demonstrace v ulicích a kde vidí cestu ke kompromisu ohledně financování veřejnoprávních médií.

items.title: Hyperscaler Heaven? A Reality Check on India’s AI Ambitions
Sources and sinks: Geoclimatic dynamics shaped the assembly of endemic fauna in the world’s Third Pole
items.summary_raw: The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), a biodiversity hotspot shaped by tectonic and climatic forces, has seen significant progress in understanding its floristic origins. However, a comprehensive, multitaxon perspective on how its terrestrial fauna assembled remains lacking. Here we integrate time-calibrated phylogenies of over 20,000 species from five major groups (invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals), to reconstruct the evolutionary history of 527 terrestrial animal species endemic to the QTP. Our finding reveals that the QTP has functioned both as a center of in situ diversification and as a “biogeographic sink” that receives species from surrounding regions, however, with pronounced subregional differentiation: the Hengduan Mountains acted primarily as a diversification source, while the Himalaya and the Plateau Platform acted as sinks, accumulating lineages from adjacent regions. The Eocene–Oligocene climatic transition, rather than late Neogene uplift, initiated sustained faunal diversification and biotic exchange. Across subregions, distinct uplift histories and monsoon regimes drove asynchronous evolutionary trajectories, showing that even geographically adjacent regions can exhibit distinct accumulation patterns of lineages. Notably, integrating our faunal evidence with recent floristic assembly data reveals a consistent “plants first, animals later” pattern across the QTP and its subregions, suggesting that early-arriving plant lineages created…

items.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders
items.summary_raw: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

items.title: Spatial reorganization during post-collapse population growth suggests conspecific attraction in baleen whale nursing grounds
items.summary_raw: Habitat use is strongly interlinked with population dynamics and plays an important role in population regulation. Animals frequently modify their habitat use behavior in response to major changes in population density. This is well studied in contexts wherein resources are limiting: for example, when changes in habitat use behavior reduce pressure from resource limitations. Situations wherein resource limitations are relaxed, such as upon recovery from severe declines, remain poorly studied. Here, we study how the spatial distribution of a nearly extirpated animal population changed during population recovery. We study a population of southern right whales ( Eubalaena australis ), a migratory species that was nearly extirpated by whaling. Using large-scale annual aerial survey data (1976–2023), we assess how spatial distribution patterns at nursing grounds changed as annual coastal abundances grew from few individuals to a few hundred. This includes assessment of the species’ characteristic site fidelity at a uniquely large spatiotemporal scale. We observed weaker fidelity to specific sites than generally assumed for Australian southern right whales and found strong indications that conspecific attraction influences the species’ coastal habitat selection. Distribution patterns initially displayed strong dispersal but became increasingly clustered coincident with substantial growth in annual whale abundances. This transition captures a rare example of a population crossing a…

items.title: Decoding climate anomalies—From scientifically sound to societally relevant
items.summary_raw: As climate impacts worsen, decision-makers, researchers, and public sector institutions increasingly need reliable, relevant, and appropriate information about emerging weather and climate anomalies. However, with the ever-expanding choice of datasets based on ground observations, satellite data, and models, it is critical to not only use the best dataset for a specific decision-making need but to avoid misinforming and even derailing decision-making due to dataset selection. The main objective of this perspective is to illustrate the importance of understanding datasets used to translate climate data into actionable knowledge, supporting the next generation of science- and data-driven climate risk management instruments, projects, and global initiatives. Through the lens of three use cases, we illustrate what data quality means for different applications, the implications of choosing, aggregating, and combining different climate datasets, and the potential consequences of dataset and baseline choice on decision-making. Choosing different datasets often leads to trade-offs that decision-makers need to be aware of, for instance, between the spatial resolution of a dataset and length of the data record. Here, we discuss the implications of selecting the appropriate time step, resolution, and dataset and provide examples of how these choices affect the identification of societally relevant anomalies.

items.title: Predicting birth weights in West Africa using subseasonal to seasonal climate and socioeconomic variables shows potential for an early warning system
items.summary_raw: Past research has shown a negative impact of climate extremes on child birth weight (BW), which is modulated by household socioeconomic and individual maternal conditions as well as the timing and degree of exposure. This study tests the potential of predicting BW using subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) climate predictors and socioeconomic indicators to support early warning systems for BW. Three sets of predictors were tested: a) a suite of biological and socioeconomic indicators from the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), b) S2S climate predictors, and c) a combination of climate predictors and selected socioeconomic indicators. The most accurate models incorporated the full set of DHS variables [predictors set (a)], with within-country (models trained and tested on the same country) predictive errors ranging from 13.5 to 17% for Burkina Faso and 20 to 25% for Mali. Cross-country (models trained on one country and tested on others) errors varied from 14 to 21% in Burkina Faso to 20 to 26% in Senegal. Models using only climate predictors [predictors set (b)] showed comparable skill to those using the full set of DHS indicators, with a relative error difference of 1 to 5%. The predictive skill was highest for children born with the most in-utero exposure to the lean season (months between planting and harvest). The results of this study have important implications for the prospect of implementing child BW early warning systems in data-sparse regions, based solely on climate…

items.title: Equity dimensions of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards: Long-term spatial population projections for New York City consistent with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
items.summary_raw: Projections of future population are important for a myriad of reasons. Large cities, states, and countries routinely produce near- and mid-range population projections. In the context of climate change, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) framework is used at global and national scales to project long-term population to inform future emissions scenarios and understand future climate-related exposures and impacts. Much less consideration has been given to long-term projections at smaller scales, even though climate impacts are place based and cities now host most of the world’s population. Cities and their metropolitan regions are complex, heterogeneous in terms of population, environmental, and built features. Thus, using global or national-scale approaches overlooks important aspects of urban futures. Cities are diverse, fluid population centers home to migrants, with employment opportunities yet substantial inequality. These quintessential city-centric features are ignored in global/national-scale population projection methods, including long-term ones consistent with the SSPs. Leveraging state-level SSP-based projections, here we extend that approach for New York City, currently home to 8.8 million persons. Combining multistate and multiregional demographic projection and spatial downscaling models, we project county-level population by racial/ethnic groups and age–sex to 2100 and downscale to 100 m. Such projections allow for an equity lens to inform assessments of…

items.title: Position-specific isotope signatures evolve during a reversible reaction
items.summary_raw: Position-specific isotope distributions capture information about reaction dynamics, metabolism, and environmental processes, encoding the formation history of organic molecules. Kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects are fundamental drivers of isotope fractionation, yet how these effects are expressed in position-specific isotope distributions remains poorly constrained. Here, we use glucose mutarotation as a model reaction for tracking the evolution of position-specific isotope ratios in a system in disequilibrium. In aqueous solution, α- and β-glucose interconvert through a low-abundance open-chain intermediate, providing an ideal framework for probing isotope effects within a single molecular pool at natural 13 C abundance. Using NMR spectroscopy, we simultaneously measure glucose anomer populations and position-specific 13 C/ 12 C ratios, enabling direct, time-resolved observations of isotope fractionation at the anomeric (C1) carbon. Starting from α-glucose, initial β-glucose formation generates a large transient isotope disequilibrium driven by unequal forward and reverse kinetic isotope effects, producing a temporary divergence in 13 C abundance of more than 30‰ between anomers. Continued interconversion redistributes the isotopes and yields an equilibrium difference of ~7‰ between α- and β-glucose at the C1 position. Together, these results demonstrate how kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects acting within a reversible reaction can generate substantial…

items.title: Correction for Ma et al., miR-182 targeting reprograms tumor-associated macrophages and limits breast cancer progression
Correction for Kawamura, Proof of the density threshold conjecture for pinwheel scheduling
In vitro binding energies capture Klf4 occupancy across the human genome
items.summary_raw: Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding to specific genomic loci determined by DNA sequence. Their sequence specificity is commonly summarized by a consensus binding motif. However, eukaryotic genomes contain billions of low-affinity DNA sequences to which TFs associate with a sequence-dependent binding energy. We currently lack insight into how the genomic sequence defines this spectrum of binding energies and the resulting pattern of TF localization. Here, we set out to obtain a quantitative understanding of sequence-dependent TF binding to both motif and nonmotif sequences. We achieve this by first pursuing accurate measurements of physical binding energies of human TF Krüppel-like factor 4 (Klf4) to a library of short DNA sequences in a fluorescence-anisotropy-based bulk competitive binding assay. Second, we show that the highly nonlinear sequence dependence of Klf4 binding energies can be captured by combining a linear model of binding energies with an Ising model of the coupled recognition of nucleotides by a TF. In this model, nucleotide–TF interfaces collectively switch between two states, weak binding and strong nucleotide-specific binding, and the states of neighboring interfaces are coupled with J ∼ 2 k B T . We find that this statistical mechanics model parameterized by our in vitro measurements captures Klf4 binding patterns on an individual long DNA molecule stretched in the optical tweezer, and is predictive for Klf4 occupancy across…

items.title: A spatially deployable iron redox rheostat tunes root growth under nutritional stress
items.summary_raw: Root growth must continuously adjust to fluctuating nutrient availability, yet the mechanisms that quantitatively integrate environmental signals into developmental responses remain poorly understood. Distinct nutrient stresses, including ammonium toxicity and phosphate deficiency, inhibit primary root growth through iron-dependent processes, suggesting that iron acts as a central regulatory node. Here, we show that plants use an antagonistic module composed of CYBDOM ferrireductases and LPR ferroxidases to regulate apoplastic iron homeostasis and control root growth in a graded manner. Genetic perturbation of this module demonstrates that root growth inhibition scales quantitatively with iron accumulation, supporting a proportional control mechanism rather than a binary response. Loss of CYBDOM function causes excessive iron accumulation, elevated reactive oxygen species, and impaired meristem activity, whereas increased CYBDOM activity buffers iron deposition and confers resistance to stress. Mechanistically, iron-induced oxidative stress promotes HYP1 expression, which in turn limits further iron accumulation. Transcriptomic analyses distinguish ammonium-specific responses from Fe-associated transcriptional changes enriched in redox buffering and cell-wall remodeling. Finally, we show that this regulatory module is redeployed in distinct tissues under phosphate deficiency, indicating that plants reuse a conserved iron-based mechanism to coordinate growth across…

items.title: Humid-heat shifts conceptions and increases pregnancy termination risks in Nigeria
items.summary_raw: Climate change is increasing the occurrence of dangerous heat events globally with immediate health consequences, particularly in the Global South. In this paper, we spatially integrate Demographic and Healt 9 h surveys with a high-resolution, blended remotely sensed and station-derived dataset of humid-heat events spanning 1983–2016 to examine the effect of humid-heat exposure on fertility in Nigeria, one of the largest and most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. We use discrete-time models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and conception probability and linear probability models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and pregnancy termination (spontaneous and induced). We find that a 1 ° C increase in the current maximum wet bulb globe temperature decreases conceptions (0.2 conceptions per 1,000 woman-months, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.4), but exposure to hotter temperatures 1 to 2 mo prior increases conception probability. Exposure to hot-humid temperatures during pregnancy increases probability of pregnancy termination (1.73 terminations per 100 pregnancies, 95% CI: 0.7 to 2.7). The net effect is an increase in births, but the timing may be shifted. Subgroup analyses reveal that effects of humid-heat on conception were larger for women residing in rural areas or in northern districts, or who are Muslim or have lower educational attainment, while the association between humid-heat and pregnancy termination was larger for women in…

Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China
items.summary_raw: The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in…

items.title: Spontaneous replication fork collapse regulates telomere length homeostasis in wild-type yeast
items.summary_raw: In most eukaryotes, the enzyme telomerase maintains the termini of linear chromosomes through the addition of repetitive telomeric sequences. It is widely assumed that the primary site of action for telomerase is the single-stranded G-rich overhang at the ends of linear chromosomes. However, increasing evidence indicates that a second telomerase substrate is generated in response to replication stress as the replisome traverses duplex telomeric DNA. We show here that this second substrate, created by spontaneous replication fork collapse in wild-type budding yeast, is elongated by telomerase at a much higher frequency than fully replicated chromosome termini. Furthermore, as much as ~200 nucleotides can be added in a single cell division to newly collapsed forks, indicating that replication fork collapse and the subsequent response by telomerase is a major determinant of telomere length homeostasis. This challenges a long-standing model which posits a length-sensing mechanism that assesses individual telomeres to determine whether yeast chromosome ends are in “telomerase-extendible” versus “telomerase-non-extendible” states. We propose that these two states are instead structurally and temporally distinct substrates for telomerase, generated by two different processes (fork collapse versus completion of DNA replication). We also show that fork collapse at telomeres is kept in check by a telomere-dedicated Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1 complex in collaboration with the canonical RPA…

items.title: New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming
items.summary_raw: Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC–MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera , but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe -associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe -associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe -derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although…

items.title: Restructuring the nitrogen cycle and sparing cropland by feeding insect-derived protein to global livestock
Solid-state laser refrigeration of nanoscale quantum sensors
items.summary_raw: Photothermal heating remains a major challenge during the optical excitation of nanoscale quantum sensors [C. Bradac, S. F. Lim, H. C. Chang, I. Aharonovich, Adv. Opt. Mater. 8 , 2000183 (2020)]. At low laser powers, heating of the sensor leads to the thermal drift of quantum electronic transition energies. At high laser powers, sensors degrade due to thermally induced phase transitions, including melting. Here, we report a general approach for mitigating the photothermal heating of nanoscale quantum sensors through solid-state laser refrigeration of the sensors’ underlying substrate. Experimentally, both nanodiamonds and gold nanocrystals are attached separately to a ceramic laser-cooling substrate through van der Waals interaction. A combination of Debye–Waller factor thermometry and optically detected magnetic resonance spectroscopy of nitrogen vacancy centers is used to demonstrate that solid-state laser refrigeration of the substrate can reduce the temperature of attached nanodiamond payloads by 25 ± 3 K below steady-state operating temperatures. Stokes/anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy is used to demonstrate reduced photothermal heating of plasmonic gold nanocrystals by 8.8 ± 2.7 K during surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy sensing of rhodamine-6G molecules. These results suggest that solid-state laser cooling could open up experimental possibilities for rapid feedback-controlled cooling of a wide range of nanoscale quantum resources.

items.title: Evaluation of possibly fabricated references in 500,000 science, engineering, and computing papers
items.summary_raw: References to nonexistent studies are well documented in biomedical research, but evidence outside biomedicine is limited. We analyzed a stratified random sample of 500,000 peer-reviewed journal papers in chemistry, physics, materials science, engineering, and computer science published from January 2023 through March 31, 2026, using OpenAlex, a large open index of scholarly works and citations. Our automated pipeline classified 1,135 references across 619 papers as fabricated, with 85.8% precision on masked expert review; fabricated is an operational label for a claimed title that could not be located in any of seven bibliographic and open-web sources. Affected-paper prevalence rose from 1 in 1,600 (6.3 per 10,000) in 2023 to 1 in 435 (23.0 per 10,000) in the first quarter of 2026, and full-period rates differed roughly sixfold across fields, from 25.6 per 10,000 papers in physics to 4.3 in chemistry. Most affected papers contained one or two fabricated references, but the 27 papers containing five or more accounted for more than a third of all fabricated references identified. Applying each field’s rate to the approximately 7 million OpenAlex papers indexed in these fields gives an estimated 8,500 papers carrying at least one fabricated reference. Routine automated reference verification at submission, together with retrospective screening of the published literature, can detect fabricated references before and after they enter the scientific record.

FMRI-guided focal transcranial magnetic stimulation of anterior cingulate cortex reduces opioid seeking and restores connectivity
items.summary_raw: Relapse remains a major challenge in opioid addiction treatment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for addiction, yet results had been mixed due to empirically selected stimulation targets and limited knowledge of neural circuit engagement. Here, we used a focal rat TMS platform to test whether high-density theta-burst stimulation (hdTBS) of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a corticostriatal node implicated in opioid relapse by prior causal and longitudinal functional MRI studies, decreases relapse-like oxycodone seeking and associated circuit dysfunction. Male rats self-administered oxycodone intravenously for 14 d and then underwent 13 d of electric barrier-induced abstinence, a procedure that suppresses drug taking while preserving drug availability and drug-associated context. During abstinence, the rats received seven daily sessions of sham stimulation or ACC-targeted hdTBS, with relapse tests and longitudinal functional MRI acquired during early and late abstinence to assess the behavioral and circuit-level effects of stimulation. Sham-treated rats showed a time-dependent increase (incubation) in oxycodone seeking and reduced ACC connectivity with dorsal and ventral striatum. In contrast, ACC-targeted hdTBS prevented incubation of oxycodone seeking and reversed abstinence-associated ACC-striatal connectivity reductions. Stimulation-sensitive functional circuits showed spatial correspondence with tracer-defined…

items.title: Populations, exposures and outcomes: How social media data is poised to advance climate-demography research
items.summary_raw: As the natural environment continues to change, there is a shared sense among researchers, policymakers, and health practitioners that we need to better understand the impacts of those changes on health and health behaviors for individuals and populations. “Big” social media data, including large datasets from platforms like X (formerly Twitter), Reddit, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube, provide access to previously hard-to-reach populations. These data are posed to revolutionize the data landscape in climate change research; however, there are limitations and ethical concerns with data from these platforms, such as ethical questions, biases, noise, and a distinct underrepresentation of marginalized groups. These issues could hamper the adoption of social media data in research on climate change and health. In this commentary, we propose leveraging and augmenting a “human-in-the-loop” approach that uses humans in data extraction, quality assurances, and model testing to ensure data quality and overcome known limitations of social media data. Using examples from health data, we propose new horizons in climate change health research made possible with qualitative research methods.

items.title: The scope and severity of bat fatalities at US wind energy facilities
items.summary_raw: Wind turbines are a major source of bat fatalities in the United States, yet the magnitude and species-specific patterns of these fatalities have remained poorly quantified because monitoring has been site-specific, unstandardized, and not designed for landscape-level synthesis. In the most comprehensive analysis to date, we synthesized 499 postconstruction monitoring reports and developed a multispecies Bayesian hierarchical framework with an adapted N-mixture model to pool information across sites and estimate total fatalities for ten bat species across the conterminous United States from 1981 to 2024. Our analysis predicts approximately 18.7 million bat fatalities over this period, with substantially higher species-specific totals than previously estimated. Our framework provides a landscape-level analysis that can predict fatalities for unmonitored locations and years, identify landscape-level drivers of fatalities, produce a multidecade hindcast of cumulative losses due to wind energy, and map where species-specific risk is highest. Although limitations and uncertainty remain, the magnitude of predicted fatalities may be comparable to total losses from white-nose syndrome, another major threat to North American bat populations. These threats affect largely different species, suggesting their impacts may compound, but updated population-level impact assessments could reveal potential cumulative effects. Our estimates of species-specific covariate relationships with…

items.title: Resource-driven release from lag phase triggers the world’s fastest and largest coastal plant invasion
items.summary_raw: What determines the duration of invasion lag phases remains one of the major unresolved questions in invasion ecology. Lag phases are often attributed to genetic adaptation, propagule limitation, or demographic stochasticity, yet the mechanisms by which environmental conditions regulate establishment success remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the explosive expansion of Spartina alterniflora along the coast of mainland China, the most rapid plant invasion recorded globally. Combining field experiments, demographic theory, and historical invasion records, we identify resource-regulated Allee effects as a mechanism governing the invasion lag phase. Experimentally, sediment accretion substantially increases clonal propagation and sexual reproduction, weakening demographic constraints associated with establishment and accelerating the transition from sparse founder patches to highly reproductive meadows. A theoretical model reveals that sediment-driven positive feedbacks weaken demographic constraints during establishment and shorten the duration of Allee effects. Historical invasion records spanning both sides of the Pacific Ocean support the predicted negative relationship between sedimentation rate and lag-phase duration. Invasion lag phases can arise solely from interactions between species traits and environmental resource availability. Contrary to the prevailing view that Allee effects are fixed properties of species, our results show that their duration is…

items.title: Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine: Toward explainable Human–AI collaboration in painting attribution
items.summary_raw: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

items.title: Correction for Croke et al., Meta-analysis and public policy: Reconciling the evidence on deworming
Anchoring Anatolian tree-rings and Mesopotamian chronology with single-year radiocarbon patterns and ice-core evidence
items.summary_raw: The historical chronology of Mesopotamia offers a key chronological bridge to connect the Near East and eastern Mediterranean during the second millennium BCE. It is unusually rich in written records, including king lists, administrative documents, royal inscriptions, and astronomical observations. The latter offer a number of alternate possible absolute anchor points, resulting in competing high, middle, low, and ultra-low temporal frameworks. Establishing which of these is correct has consequences far beyond Mesopotamia. Tree-ring sequences from preserved timbers at archaeological sites in Anatolia, linked directly to Mesopotamia via the Old Assyrian trade network, could provide the answer. However, attempts have been limited by the lack of calendar secured dendrochronological dating for these timbers. Here we develop transferable methodologies in single-year radiocarbon analysis, utilizing patterns of 14 C preserved in single tree rings from Anatolian timbers to anchor their combined chronology 2072 BCE–744 BCE. This provides a calendrically-secured reference chronology for wood samples from Anatolian sites during this period as well as an annually resolved paleoclimatic record. Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Remaining dating uncertainties are constrained in strong support of the middle–low chronology.

items.title: Autonomous disproofs of the Erdős unit distance conjecture with GPT-5.5 Pro
items.summary_raw: OpenAI’s disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marks a milestone in AI for mathematical research. However, the result relied on an internal model with undisclosed test-time compute, hindering independent reproduction and analysis by the community. Here we present a simple autonomous agent built on the publicly available GPT-5.5 Pro. The agent uses a problem-agnostic three-stage prompting pipeline: brainstorm, execute, and review. We ran eight independent trials with web search disabled. In each trial, the agent produced a correct or essentially correct disproof of the conjecture. The resulting proofs are diverse and do not merely reproduce earlier AI-generated proofs. Since GPT-5.5 Pro was released nearly a month before OpenAI published its disproof, our evaluation is free from data contamination. The system operates efficiently, using an average of 106.7 k reasoning tokens per trial. We release our code and all outputs, providing a publicly accessible AI agent to resolve this conjecture autonomously.

items.summary_raw: By her own admission, Marjorie Steele doesn’t get along with many people in the climate movement. She runs a Michigan-based activist group that advocates against large-scale industrial development. Though she considers herself a political independent, her opposition often puts her into conflict with both climate advocates and Trump-aligned conservatives. She spends most of her time these days focusing on data centers, but she founded the activist group Economic Development Responsibility Alliance to oppose a Chinese electric vehicle battery plant near the city of Big Rapids. She has also campaigned against solar farms, battery storage systems, and transmission lines, one of which is being built on the property adjacent to hers. “When the progressives look at me and say, ‘You’re MAGA’ because of the green energy issue, it really hurts me,” Steele told Grist. As she has crossed the state opposing new development projects, she has encountered fierce pushback from climate-conscious progressives. There has been one notable exception. Earlier this year, when she was in Lansing to lobby state lawmakers for a data center ban, she met William Lawrence, a Democrat who is running for U.S. Congress in Michigan’s 7th District. She knew that Lawrence was a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, one of the nation’s most prominent climate organizations, so she wasn’t sure how he would receive her. The two sat down to eat Jimmy John’s, and she spoke to him at length about what she sees as the…

items.title: Thwaites is a runaway climate disaster. New studies show how.
items.summary_raw: A single glacier sitting at the bottom of the world may be all that is holding back catastrophic amounts of sea level rise. As it melts away faster than ever, scientists are racing to get a better understanding of when it might fail. Unfortunately, they’ve recently found more bad news. The Antarctic bulwark known as Thwaites, or the “Doomsday Glacier,” is gargantuan — roughly the size of Florida — and holds enough ice to push the planet’s coastlines up 2 feet. But the edge of Thwaites also acts as a cork, holding up the rim of the West Antarctic ice sheet, much of which sits below sea level. As Thwaites deteriorates, more ice in this bowl becomes exposed to the ocean, creating a feedback loop that makes it melt faster. And if Thwaites were to succumb entirely, the whole interior of the sheet might follow suit, raising sea levels by as much as 10 feet. It’s easy to track Thwaites’ demise from space, but predicting its future has been much trickier. For years, computer models used to simulate Thwaites’ retreat weren’t able to pass the simple test of accurately re-creating the retreat that satellites have captured over the last few decades, marking them unreliable tools for looking ahead. But now, scientists have plugged in a major missing piece. A new paper, published in Nature Communications earlier this month , appears to be the first to account for what’s happening underneath Thwaites to simulate how quickly it may lose ice. Using this model to simulate the future paints a…

items.title: Climate change rarely goes on trial. This one could be a landmark.
items.summary_raw: Climate change gets a rare day in court today when 15 Canadian youth will accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights by failing to adequately address the country’s role in global warming. Although thousands of similar cases have been filed across the globe, legal experts said this long-awaited case is arguably the most consequential to reach trial. The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change. Like similar cases in the United States, including the landmark Held v. Montana , the plaintiffs in La Rose v. His Majesty the King argue that the government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing the crisis to continue. Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts. “It’s the chance for the young people to tell their story,” said Kelly Matheson, deputy director for global strategy at Our Children’s Trust, the nonprofit behind this case and many similar efforts around the world. The outcome, while not precedent-setting outside of Canada, could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases. “We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “This trial will be…

items.title: California has a plan for El Niño’s torrential rain: Save it for later
items.summary_raw: Something ominous just hit California: rain . The life-giving water that normally hydrates people and crops is bringing an aura of dread this autumn, thanks to the strongest El Niño ever recorded . While the phenomenon causes severe drought and heat in many parts of the world, historically it’s brought extraordinary rainfall to the Golden State. The monstrous El Niño of 1997 and 1998, for instance, caused widespread flooding and debris flows (made not just of water and dirt, but big chunks of rock), destroying property and killing residents . The state can’t stop rain from falling, so in the last few decades it has been renegotiating its relationship with precipitation. As climate change makes California whiplash from years of intense drought to years of intense rain , water agencies have been capturing as much H2O as they can to reduce reliance on using canals to bring it in from afar. That’s set the state up to avoid at least some flooding as this El Niño takes hold and bank the bounty for the dry spells to come. “Heavy storms can affect regional infrastructure, construction schedules, and areas vulnerable to debris flow or power disruptions,” said a spokesperson with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power in a statement provided to Grist. “However, these rain events also present a significant opportunity. Stormwater capture is a critical pillar of LADWP’s long-term plan to reduce reliance on purchased imported water.” The threat isn’t just more rain overall, but…
