items.title: Finite Element-Based Stress Analysis of the Main Frame of a Battery-Operated Lathyrus Harvester
items.source_name: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
items.summary_raw: Lathyrus (Lathyrus sativus L.) is a climate-resilient pulse grown mainly as a relay crop in rice fallows, but it is still harvested by hand, a slow, labour-intensive and physically demanding process. A battery-operated lathyrus harvester was therefore developed, and this study evaluated the structural safety of its main frame, the principal load-bearing component, using finite element analysis (FEA). A three-dimensional model of the frame was analysed in ANSYS Workbench 2024 R1 under static loads representing field operation, namely the weight of the battery, motor and transmission, the cutting resistance of lathyrus stems and the inertial force of the reciprocating knife. Structural steel properties were assigned, and support reactions, equivalent elastic strain, directional deformation and von Mises stress were evaluated. The maximum von Mises stress was 223.92 MPa, confined to a critical joint region and below the 250 MPa yield strength of the material, giving a minimum factor of safety of 1.12. The maximum equivalent elastic strain was 0.0011939 m/m and was limited to local stress-concentration zones, while most of the frame showed negligible strain. The frame deflected like a cantilever, with a maximum upward displacement of 11.995 mm at the free end and a maximum downward displacement of 8.913 mm near the restrained region. The frame is therefore safe against yielding under static field loads, but the narrow safety margin and the free-end deflection show that local…

items.title: Organisational Conditions for Healthcare Workers' Wellbeing: The Roles of Leadership, Social Climate and Psychosocial Safety Climate
items.summary_raw: AIM: To assess a comprehensive model linking servant leadership, health-promoting leadership, workplace social climate, psychosocial safety climate, work conditions and healthcare workers' wellbeing. DESIGN: A cross-sectional survey design. METHODS: A total of 1563 healthcare workers completed a survey between 2024 and 2025. Structural equation modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships. RESULTS: Servant leadership, health-promoting leadership and workplace social climate were positively associated with healthcare workers' perceptions of psychosocial safety climate. Higher levels of psychosocial safety climate were linked to lower cognitive job demands and greater job resources, including job control, supervisor support and colleague support. These work conditions were associated with lower psychological strain and turnover intention, as well as higher job satisfaction and work engagement. Unexpectedly, cognitive job demands were positively related to work engagement, suggesting that cognitively challenging work may be perceived as meaningful and motivating in healthcare settings. CONCLUSIONS: Supportive leadership and a positive workplace social climate are important correlates of psychosocial safety climate, which was associated with healthier work conditions and better wellbeing among healthcare workers. In addition, the findings suggest that certain job demands may play a motivational as well as a straining role in healthcare contexts. IMPLICATIONS…

items.title: Exploring the five-layer ecological model of English language teachers’ motivational (micro)climates: A descriptive qualitative study
items.summary_raw: Abstract This descriptive qualitative study explored the perceptions of 17 Iranian English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers regarding the ecological factors that construct motivational (micro) climate. The analysis of narrative frames and interview data revealed various factors at five ecological layers that shape the motivational (micro) climate. At the micro level, factors related to ‘teachers’, ‘students’, ‘classroom interactions’, ‘resources and tasks’, physical environment’, and ‘individual differences’ established motivational (micro)climate. At the meso level, ‘school/university-home relations’, ‘institutional policies’, ‘educational regulations’, ‘teacher-parent interactions’, and ‘peer and group engagement’ were highlighted. The ‘educational system’, ‘cultural values’, ‘social norms’, ‘economy’, ‘political climate’, and ‘globalization and internationalization of English’ were the macro-level factors. Concerning exo factors, ‘educational resources’, ‘community attitude and services’, ‘family’, and ‘mass media’ were emphasized. At the chrono level, ‘time passage’, ‘developmental changes’, and ‘historical events’ were underscored. Implications are provided for teachers and teacher educators to (re)consider motivational (micro) climate ecology.

items.title: Climate Change Awareness and Engagement Among Aviation Students and Organizations
items.source_name: Journal of Advanced Studies in Aviation Aerospace and Management
items.summary_raw: This study explores climate change awareness and strategic engagement among aviation students and organizations at Indiana Aerospace University during Academic Year 2024–2025. Guided by Contingency Theory, the study utilized an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design involving a structured survey of 100 participants (50 students across different year levels and 50 representatives from seven campus organizations) and follow-up qualitative interviews. Quantitative findings revealed high overall levels of knowledge regarding climate change causes and industry impacts (weighted mean = 4.31) and a strong role perception of sustainability as a professional obligation (weighted mean = 4.34). However, strategic participation scored lower (weighted mean = 4.12), highlighting a gap between student awareness and active involvement. The primary challenges encountered include difficulties committing to daily campus sustainable practices, rare participation in sustainability activities, and challenges encouraging peers to join initiatives. Qualitative data contextualized these barriers, pointing to limited awareness of campus policies, lack of motivation, and insufficient practical opportunities. The study concludes that high environmental knowledge and positive attitudes are insufficient on their own to drive action without supportive institutional frameworks. It recommends embedding sustainability and green aviation technologies directly into curricula, enhancing communication…

items.title: Decomposing Climate Policy Uncertainty and Systemic Banking Risk in the United States: Implications for Sustainable Finance
items.summary_raw: Climate policy uncertainty is usually measured as a single index, which cannot tell supervisors whether risk to banks comes from Congress, federal agencies, or international commitments. This study separates these channels. Because banks provide much of the credit needed for the low-carbon transition, knowing where this risk comes from matters for sustainable finance as well as for financial stability. We build legislative and regulatory indices that count formal attempts to block, delay, or reverse existing U.S. climate policy, alongside an international-commitment index and a market-based transition uncertainty measure. Using monthly data from January 2005 to December 2024, a quantile VAR with frequency decomposition, a time-varying model, and bias-corrected bootstrap inference, we trace spillovers to G-SIB, regional and broker-dealer equity risk, G-SIB CDS spreads, and ΔCoVaR. In normal months, climate policy uncertainty has little measurable effect on bank risk once broader financial conditions are controlled for. Spillovers emerge in the tails and build within a quarter. Regulatory reversal risk outweighs the international and market channels when bank risk rises fastest, but no more than contested legislation does. In the tails, the resolution of policy fights moves bank risk more than their outbreak, and legislative spillovers disappear when contested bills are replaced by the volume of climate legislation. Climate stress scenarios should therefore center on…

items.title: Contesting the infrastructures of attention: Climate activism and asymmetric visibility in France
items.summary_raw: Drawing on two years of ethnographic fieldwork with Extinction Rebellion Paris and allied movements, semi-structured interviews with activists, and analysis of media coverage and investigative reporting on police surveillance technology, this article examines how French climate movements have reoriented their political practice from seeking visibility within an existing media system toward contesting the infrastructures of attention through which public visibility is produced and governed. It argues that this reorientation reflects a shift in the politics of climate communication: from a logic of media access to one of infrastructural contestation, targeting media ownership and security apparatuses. The analysis examines how activists experience narratives of disorder and eco-terrorism as challenges to their political legitimacy, alongside the expansion of biometric surveillance documented by investigative reporting. It develops the concept of asymmetric visibility regimes to capture the resulting double bind, in which activists struggle for recognition in the media sphere while becoming increasingly identifiable in the security sphere. The article contributes to debates on media power, hybrid media systems, and the communicative conditions of democratic dissent.

items.title: Household Choice of Renewable Energy Sources in Kenya
items.summary_raw: Kenya recognizes the relationship between its emerging economy, energy, and the well-being of its citizens through the Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change. Kenya’s Vision 2030 points to the huge contribution of energy toward strengthening adaptability, climate resilience, and good performance in different branches of the economy. The Kenya government has established different policies and laws in a bid to decarbonize the energy sector, and with a goal of attaining complete use of the national grid, 100 percent clean energy by 2030, common access to clean cooking, 2028, gearing towards reaching Net Zero in 2050. The Nationally Determined Contribution of the country is to significantly cut down greenhouse gas emissions by 30 percent by 2030. Despite the development of these policies, the adoption of renewable energy sources among Kenyan households remains suboptimal, highlighting the need to examine the determinants of household choice of renewable energy sources. Therefore, this study sought to determine the factors influencing household choice of renewable energy sources in Kenya. A cross-sectional research design was employed in the study to assess and analyze the choice of renewable energy sources in the country. The study leveraged on secondary data from Multi-Tier Framework Survey conducted in 2016 – 2018 by the World Bank. Anchored on the Theory of Planned Behavior, the dataset provided the information required to examine the factors…

Enabling Sustainable Digital Transition in Mountain Dairy Systems: A Multiscale Farm–Territory Analysis
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Digital technologies are promoted as levers of sustainable transformation, yet their role in mountain livestock systems depends on more than technology availability. In these contexts, digitalisation is shaped by interactions between farm capabilities, resources, territorial trajectories and public support. This study analyses sustainable digital transition pathways in mountain dairy systems in the Autonomous Province of Trento, Italy, by linking farm‐level digital profiles with municipal‐level enabling conditions. A survey of 300 dairy farms was integrated with municipal data on livestock dynamics, land use for 2016–2025 and public support for 2016–2024. Farm‐level indicators captured technology adoption, awareness, perceived usefulness, future purchase intention and the adoption gap. Logistic regression and latent class analysis identified adoption drivers and digital profiles, while the Territorial Livestock Innovation Opportunity Index assessed place‐based conditions for innovation. Digitalisation was widespread but uneven. Basic‐, Medium‐ and Advanced‐equipped farms represented 52.7%, 34.7% and 12.7% of the sample. Adoption increased from 18.8% in small farms to 45.2% and 52.1% in medium and large farms, while future purchase intention was concentrated in production management (23.6%), animal monitoring (17.4%) and automation (16.9%). Municipal CTAI, FPII and TLIOI values ranged from 0 to 0.762, 0 to 0.690 and 0.125 to 0.478, revealing mismatches between…

items.title: Heterogeneous impacts of temperature extremes on climate attitudes and Green voting
items.summary_raw: In the past decade, the public in Europe has become more concerned about climate change and expresses stronger proenvironmental policy preferences. Based on data from the European Social Survey (2012-2022, 25 countries), we show that the increased exposure to temperature extremes has contributed to the observed changes in climate change attitudes and electoral support for environmentalist policy platforms. For each additional degree of excess temperature experienced during warm spells measured over the previous 12 mo, we find that the probabilities of being worried about climate change, of feeling responsible for climate change, and of voting for Green parties and Green coalitions increase by 4.0 [CI95: 2.5, 5.5], 2.5 [CI95: 1.1, 3.9], and 2.8 [CI95: 0.9, 3.7] percentage points respectively. We also document significant heterogeneity across individuals, based on gender and education, particularly between highly educated women and low-educated men. While the latter group consistently exhibits the lowest proenvironmental attitudes and voting, it is this group that shows the strongest increases when exposed to temperature extremes, converging toward the levels of their more educated counterparts. Further regional heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects of warm temperature extremes are smaller in less prosperous or economically disadvantaged regions, as well as in regions with greenhouse gas emission levels above the median. The findings suggest a nuanced interplay…

items.title: The impact of Trumpism upon the European Green Deal
items.summary_raw: Abstract The article, based on theoretical and empirical analysis, provides a deeper understanding of the content, scale, and potential of Trumpism as a strategic challenge to the European Green Deal (EGD). Through interdisciplinary and comparative approaches, methods of political ecology, neo-cleavage theory and case study, the impact of Trumpism on the implementation prospects for the EGD is investigated. Particular emphasis is placed on the Trumpist challenge to the global scope and substance of European climate policy. The notable consolidation of pro-Trumpist parties’ influence within the European Parliament and national legislatures of EU member states during the 2020s, particularly since 2024, coupled with their capacity to affect climate policy decision-making through coalition agreements and enhanced collaboration with mainstream centre-right parties, augments intra-structural risks to the implementation of the EGD and poses a substantial threat to the climate consensus at the EU level, potentially jeopardizing the EGD’s continuity in the medium term. Since the relevant economic development plans and roadmaps for Ukraine’s integration into the EU are related to the EGD objectives and taking into account long-lasting effects of the full-scale Russian invasion, there is a need for a more systemic and critical look at the prospects for a gradual increase in taxation of CO2 emissions and fossil fuels in Ukraine as well as its transition to the EU Carbon Border…

items.title: Public acceptance of new hydrogen production technologies: A comparative study in Germany
items.summary_raw: Green hydrogen has significant potential to support the energy transition. However, limited deployment of new hydrogen technologies, means that non-technical, system-level factors may constrain the large-scale implementation of hydrogen systems. Using a survey in Germany (n = 1201), this study examines awareness and social acceptance considerations for two emerging green hydrogen technologies: electrically assisted gasification (eGas); and reversible solid oxide cells (rSOC). The results indicate that the predictors of acceptance are similar across the technologies with Perceived cost, perceived benefits and perceived safety showing the strongest associations with acceptance. However, respondents expressed significantly higher local acceptance for rSOC facilities than for eGas. This suggests that the public's responses to hydrogen are influenced by the characteristics of specific system configurations rather than hydrogen as a generic energy carrier. These findings reinforce the importance of assessing perceived cost, safety and benefits implications when considering technology selection and siting. The study identifies implementation and policy implications for eGas and rSOC systems, which are relevant for technology developers as well as planners and decision-makers who are seeking to support the practical rollout of green hydrogen infrastructure.

items.title: Techno-economic analysis (TEA) of partial and full electrification of clinker production
Corporate Climate Transition Accountability in International Law: Legalisation, Climate Justice and the Asian Global Value-Chain Perspective
items.source_name: International Law Review (Centro Universitario de Brasilia)
items.summary_raw: This article examines whether the legalisation of corporate climate transition accountability advances climate justice, particularly for developing Asian economies embedded in global value chains. It uses doctrinal, comparative and normative analysis to trace four regulatory pathways: climate disclosure, due diligence, transition planning and access to remedy. The article argues that the movement from soft-law standards to hard-law duties is neither linear nor sufficient. International instruments have supplied a common vocabulary of responsibility, due diligence and transition planning, yet their translation into EU, US and Asian frameworks remains fragmented and politically unstable. The article concludes that climate justice will not be secured by soft law alone, nor by rigid extraterritorial hard law that shifts compliance costs to suppliers and developing host States. A just model requires a hard-law floor - enforceable disclosure, climate due diligence, stakeholder participation and remedies - supported by soft-law technical standards, capacity building and climate finance. Its originality lies in reframing corporate climate transition accountability from an investor-centred disclosure project into a rights-holder-centred accountability framework.

items.title: Preparing for Tomorrow: Tools, Skills, and Sensors in Forecasting Climate Change's Health Consequences
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Introduction. Climate change has important implications for human health. Temperatures continue to rise and extreme weather conditions become more frequent. Resulting changes in ecosystems will impact health in general and more specifically, distribution of communicable, vector-borne and heat-related diseases. It is imperative to adopt proactive measures to anticipate and mitigate the health impact of climate change. New sensors, skills and tools are required to predict impact on human health and conceptualise proactive measures against adverse consequences of rising temperatures. Materials and methods. A search of the current literature on anticipatory research specific to sensors, skills and tools for prediction was employed. A design thinking model, the ClimateSense Model was conceptualised based on the analysis. Results. Sensors include physical sensors and information technology such as remote sensing with satellites, aircrafts and drones, biological sensors like RNA and DNA sequencing technologies, and chemical sensors for greenhouse gases. Tools include mobile applications and artificial intelligence, internet-of-things technology, and crowdsourcing. Skills involve digital skills to interpret and communicate sensor-derived data using interactive maps, plots, time series, and analysis of big data with statistical skills or artificial intelligence. Conclusion. Synergistic combination of tools, skills and sensors, as conceptualised in the ClimateSense model, are…

items.title: Optimizing cross-border CCS policy: an integrated energy–carbon–cost framework for source–host credit allocation
items.summary_raw: Cross-border carbon capture and storage (CCS) can support industrial decarbonisation where emissions and storage resources are unevenly distributed. Existing optimisation studies mainly minimise techno-economic cost and rarely integrate energy penalties, country-level emissions accounting, domestic-versus-export allocation, and source–host credit sharing. This study develops a mixed-integer linear programming framework that selects domestic or export storage, shipping routes, offshore pipelines, and sinks while tracking operational emissions, costs, and source–host credit allocation. An anonymised Japan–Malaysia case includes two Japanese sources, two Malaysian sinks, and a domestic screening pathway. Domestic Japanese storage costs USD 0.327 billion/year, compared with USD 0.484 billion/year for full export. Under the Combined Competitiveness scenario, a combination of a lower Malaysian service fee, equal source–host credit sharing, and an upper-end published domestic-storage cost selects full export to MY-Sink 1 at USD 0.426 billion/year, with the capability of storing 2.674 MtCO2/year after shipping loss. Credit ownership changes economic and national accounting outcomes without changing routing. Malaysian storage and injection, shipping, and credit values give the largest local sensitivity responses. In summary, the framework provides a transparent method for assessing cross-border CCS competitiveness, operational emissions, and sink selection.

items.title: Developing a climate responsive X minute city framework for walkability planning in Bahrain
items.summary_raw: The cities of the Gulf area are in a paradoxical position as they are small enough for proximity-based planning and yet are hostile to walking because of the climate. This paper develops a conceptual Climate-Responsive X-Minute City (CRXMC) framework for examining how walkability-oriented planning can be adapted to the climatic and socio-spatial conditions of Bahrain, one of the small and highly urbanized states with temperatures that frequently exceed 40 °C, and car dependency is deeply rooted in the physical and cultural fabric of life. In recognition of the fact that the traditional proximity models cannot be implemented directly in the hot-arid environments, the paper proposes the new framework of Climate-Responsive X-Minute City (CRXMC) that revisits the concept of accessibility beyond the spatial proximity and includes thermal comfort and climatic usability. The study uses an integrative review of minute-city scholarship, climate-responsive urbanism and Gulf urbanism, supported by a comparative analysis of selected international and GCC initiatives, policy interpretation and an illustrative GIS-based accessibility diagnostic for Salman City. The GIS analysis maps network-based walking access to selected essential services and transit stops within 5-, 10-, and X-minute thresholds, and organizes the Barrier Solution Actor matrix in Salman City, Bahrain. The resulting framework identifies six interconnected planning dimensions: neighbourhood accessibility, land-use…

items.title: Comparative Assessment of Climate Change Impacts and Farmers’ Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices in Tropical Crops Production Systems in Davao Oriental, Philippines
items.summary_raw: Climate change increasingly threatens tropical crop production through erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, and more frequent extreme weather events that reduce crop productivity and disrupt farm management. This study assessed climate change impacts and farmers’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) across banana, cassava, and mixed-cropping systems in Davao Oriental, Philippines. A total of 450 farmers were surveyed using a structured questionnaire, and data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Banana farmers perceived the greatest climate change impacts (mean = 4.35), followed by cassava (4.05) and mixed-crop farmers (3.98). Across all systems, farmers demonstrated moderate to high knowledge (3.55–3.85) and positive attitudes (3.70–4.10) toward climate change adaptation, yet adaptation practices remained only moderate (3.50–3.75). Major climate-related challenges included erratic rainfall, prolonged drought, flooding, increasing pest and disease incidence, and declining crop yields. Common adaptation strategies included crop diversification, supplemental irrigation, drought-tolerant planting materials, soil conservation, and improved pest management. However, about 20% of banana farmers reported adopting no adaptation measures. Climate change affected not only crop productivity but also planting schedules, water management, and crop protection. Production constraints also varied by landscape, with upland banana and…

items.title: Saudi Arabian and Emirati Climate Diplomacy toward Pacific Island Countries: Motivations, Practices, and Limits
items.summary_raw: Why do hydrocarbon-exporting states pursue climate diplomacy toward Pacific Island countries that call for an accelerated fossil-fuel transition? This article compares Saudi Arabian and Emirati engagement from 2010 to September 2026 through a qualitative analysis of official documents, regional communiques, climate-policy texts, project records, and scholarly literature. It combines status seeking, niche diplomacy, institutional assets, and recipient agency in a framework linking motivations, practices, and outcomes. The findings show that economic diversification, reputational pressures, and wider South-South engagement motivate both states, but their institutional resources generate different diplomatic pathways. The United Arab Emirates follows a project-technology-institution model based on renewable-energy delivery, specialized agencies, and multilateral platforms. Saudi Arabia follows a finance-forum-politics model centered on major pledges, ministerial convening, and high-level diplomatic outreach. Pacific Island countries filter both approaches through regional priorities, partnership rules, and fossil-fuel-free norms. Consequently, Gulf engagement has produced tangible functional benefits and some institutional access, but limited normative convergence. The article argues that climate finance becomes diplomatic influence only when commitments are implemented, embedded in Pacific-led institutions, and judged consistent with recipient-defined climate priorities. It…

items.title: Congestion pricing as an urban energy strategy: a mixed-methods analysis of expert insights on regional implementation challenges and energy trade-offs
items.summary_raw: Congestion pricing (CP) is increasingly promoted as a demand-side instrument to manage urban congestion, reduce transport energy use, and advance climate goals. Yet adoption remains geographically uneven and politically contested, raising questions about how practitioners assess its feasibility and energy relevance. This study provides a cross-regional policy analysis of expert perspectives on CP as an energy and mobility strategy. Drawing on 107 qualitative responses from transportation and energy professionals in North America, Europe, the Middle East, and the Rest of the World (RoW), the study integrates deductive thematic coding, stance classification, network analysis, and sentiment scoring. Results show that inadequate transit alternatives were the most consistently cited barrier across all regions (35–36%), highlighting CP’s dependence on complementary infrastructure investment. Other barriers vary regionally: public acceptance is the most frequently mentioned barrier in North America (39%) and Europe (55%). Other prominent concerns include infrastructure gaps in North America (29%), political resistance in Europe (36%) and RoW (32%), and infrastructure gaps (29%) and economic conditions (26%) in the Middle East. Only 28% of the 100 respondents who provided substantive answers to Question 2 consider CP independently decisive for energy reduction, while 18% dismiss its significance entirely; the majority (54%) adopt conditional or nuanced positions, framing its impact…

items.title: NARRATIVE WARFARE AND MEDIA FRAMING IN THE PAHALGAM INCIDENT: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF INDIAN, PAKISTANI AND WESTERN MEDIA DISCOURSE
items.summary_raw: The attack on the city of Pahalgam in 22 April 2025, which resulted in the death of 26 people in Indian-administered Kashmir, had a dramatic effect on the India–Pakistan relations, leading to a sudden deterioration in the relations between the two countries and finally to armed clashes in May 2025. The study explores the competing narratives created by Indian, Pakistani and western media about the incident and ensuing crisis. The study is based on Framing Theory, Agenda-Setting Theory and the notion of narrative warfare and adopts a qualitative comparative discourse analysis to analyze the source selection, the attribution of responsibility, lexical selection, thematic emphasis, representation of terrorism, national identity, and military and diplomatic reaction. The results show that there are significant differences between the three media environments. The media in India mainly portrayed the issue in terms of national security, terrorism, victimization and threat from Pakistan narratives. The emphasis of the Pakistani media was on denial, uncertainty of facts, Kashmir's political status which is yet to be resolved and fear of possible exploitation by the Indian side. The Western media more often took an attribution-sensitive and de-escalatory tone, focusing on human rights issues, conflicting claims, the Kashmir issue and escalation dangers between the two nuclear nations. The study has shown that news media were not only spatiotemporal platforms for exchanging…

items.title: An approach to improving the climate resilience and environmental sustainability of primary care facilities in Cederberg sub-district
items.summary_raw: Aim Primary care facilities in South Africa face growing risks from climate change and environmental degradation, yet practical tools to strengthen local resilience remain limited. This article describes a participatory approach to assessing and improving the climate resilience and environmental sustainability of primary care facilities in the Cederberg sub-district, Western Cape. Method The project adapted the Health Facility Climate Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (VCA) tool developed by the Climate Action Accelerator and complemented it with a carbon footprint evaluation using the Climate Impact Checkup tool from Health Care Without Harm. The VCA followed five steps: (1) a desk review to identify climate hazards and contextual vulnerabilities; (2) a facility audit across four WHO domains (workforce; water, sanitation and waste; energy; and infrastructure); (3) focus group tabletop discussions to explore responses to climate events; (4) synthesis of findings into a risk and solution matrix; and (5) prioritisation of feasible interventions. The process engaged healthcare workers and managers across six facilities and generated 43 potential solutions, 14 of which were prioritised for implementation. Findings The VCA fostered awareness, collaboration, and action planning for climate resilience, while the carbon audit highlighted pathways for emissions reduction. items.title: The Visibility Bargain: The Psychological Costs of Sustained Public Climate Communication
items.summary_raw: Abstract: As climate change has moved from a scientific concern to a highly visible societal and political issue, climate scientists have increasingly been called upon to serve as public interpreters of climate risk. Expectations that scientists engage with media, counter misinformation, and participate in public debate have expanded alongside their existing research, teaching, and administrative responsibilities. Yet despite the growing normalization of public engagement as a professional obligation, the psychological consequences of sustained scientific visibility remain insufficiently theorized within psychology. This article provides a conceptual synthesis of psychological and interdisciplinary research to examine the consequences of sustained public climate communication. Integrating research on emotional labor, moral injury, and occupational stress, it introduces the concept of the visibility bargain: an implicit institutional arrangement through which expectations of public engagement redistribute emotional and ethical burdens from institutions to individual scientists. Drawing on qualitative research, case studies, and communication scholarship, the article argues that for climate scientists, sustained public visibility may be associated with cumulative emotional strain, ethical dissonance, exposure to harassment, and career vulnerability. items.title: Climate Risk Perception and Household Adaptation Behaviour in Climate-Vulnerable Coastal Communities of Bangladesh
items.source_name: Journal of risk analysis and crisis response
items.summary_raw: Household adaptation is crucial for building the resilience of coastal communities in Bangladesh, which face a high risk of impacts on their livelihoods and well-being due to climate change. This research aims to examine the behavioural determinants of household adaptation, and combines Protection Motivation Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour. It specifically focuses on the impact of climate risk perception, environmental knowledge, self-efficacy, and perceived response effectiveness on household adaptation behaviour by taking into account the mediating role of adaptation intention and the moderating role of community resilience. The data were taken from 230 households from six climate-vulnerable coastal districts (Khulna, Satkhira, Bagerhat, Barguna, Patuakhali, and Bhola) using a structured questionnaire with 5-point Likert scale items. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the proposed model. The results indicate that climate risk perception, environmental knowledge, self-efficacy, and perceived response effectiveness are significant factors that positively contribute to the formation of adaptation intention, which then determines household adaptation behaviour. The four antecedent variables' relationships with adaptation behaviour are also found to be significantly mediated by the variable adaptation intention. items.title: Climate change and agribusiness entrepreneurship in Tanzania: The mediating role of adaptation strategies
items.summary_raw: Agribusiness entrepreneurship in Tanzania operates within a climate-vulnerable agricultural economy in which rising temperatures, erratic rainfall and recurrent extreme weather events threaten production and business continuity. However, the mechanism through which climate change is transmitted into entrepreneurial outcomes specifically the role played by adaptation strategies remains empirically under examined in the Tanzanian context. This study therefore pursued two objectives: (i) to examine the direct effect of climate change on agribusiness entrepreneurship, and (ii) to assess the mediating role of adaptation strategies in this relationship, drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory to frame adaptation strategies as capability-building responses to environmental disruption. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed to collect primary data from 252 agribusiness entrepreneurs (smallholder farmers, small and medium enterprises, and start-ups) in Morogoro and Dodoma regions, selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model satisfied recommended thresholds for indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity and discriminant validity. items.title: How much development aid is spent on climate change?
items.summary_raw: Around one-fifth of development aid is spent on climate-related projects. But what does climate-related mean, and does it crowd out other aid projects?

items.title: Civic Education in the Context of the Challenge of Climate Change
items.summary_raw: The article presents the challenges of civic education and a civic upbringing in the era of the transforming of society in response to climate change.These challenges include not only support for mitigation and adaptation measures but also support for maintaining or deepening democratic processes and institutions.Following the UNESCO call for educational transformation (2021), responsible civic education was defined as education that leads students to support pro-climate measures (a shared truth and a vision of the future) but also to embrace democratic civil attitudes.According to UNESCO, education should lead to peaceful activism that criticises and confronts the power structures that disrupt or prevent shared truths about a possible future.The authors therefore describe the transformations in civil disobedience (CD) and theoretical reflections on CD that appreciate its importance and potential for promoting pro-climatic measures.They also present other civil approaches and examples of addressing the climate crisis, specifically examining the democratic limits and positive aspects of the concepts of environmental and ecological citizenship, deliberative democracy, and eco-modernism.They then present the concepts of civic education and offer answers to the question of what parameters responsible civic education should meet.First, they show the current interdependence between the subject of civic education and climate change.They then present Westheimer's models of civic…

items.title: Perceptions of risk and investment in wind energy in rural communities
items.summary_raw: This study examines whether individual risk attitudes, investment preferences and socio-economic characteristics are associated with stated willingness to invest in onshore wind-energy projects among rural respondents in Tanzania, with Ireland retained as a complementary case from a more established wind-energy market. Using ordered and generalised ordered logistic regression models, the Tanzanian results reveal substantial investment interest, with approximately half of respondents indicating willingness to invest. However, neither self-rated nor assessed risk consistently predicts investment propensity, while most financial, attitudinal and socio-demographic variables show weak or threshold-specific associations. In the complementary Irish sample, self-rated risk is positively and consistently associated with investment propensity, whereas assessed risk is substantially weaker. Required returns and selected individual characteristics are also associated with particular investment thresholds. Overall, the findings suggest that individual risk attitudes alone provide an incomplete explanation of prospective wind-energy investment in Tanzania. Policies should therefore consider accessible investment structures, credible information and greater opportunities for exposure to wind-energy projects, while future research should directly examine financial, institutional and project-level factors not captured in this study.

items.title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
items.summary_raw: Abstract In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.
